s: The fifth letter of the German alphabet, written in the Latin script.
used to form nouns from adjectives, sometimes with umlaut of the root vowel; the nouns express the quality of the adjective
stark (“strong”) + -e → Stärke (“strength”)
-e.et: From Middle High German -e, from Old High German -ī, from Proto-Germanic *-į̄.

s: used to form feminine nouns from verbs: forms instrument nouns
anzeigen (“to display, indicate”) + -e → Anzeige (“display, advert”)
durchreichen (“to hand through, pass through”) + -e → Durchreiche (“hatch, passthrough”)
used to form feminine nouns from verbs: forms action nouns
colloquial
abzocken (“to rip off”) + -e → Abzocke (“rip-off”)
denken (“to think”) + -e → Denke (“way of thinking, mentality”)
used to form two-syllable clippings from feminine nouns
colloquial
Frisur (“haircut”) + -e → Frise
Putzfrau (“female cleaner”) + -e → Putze
-e.et: From Middle High German -e, from a merger of various Old High German vocalic noun endings.

s: used to form the plural of some nouns; usually triggering umlaut of the root vowel in masculines and feminines, but not in neuters
Baum (“tree”) + -e → Bäume (“trees”)
Nacht (“night”) + -e → Nächte (“nights”)
used to form the dative of strong masculine and neuter nouns ending in a stressed syllable
das Haus (“house”) → dem Hause (usually: dem Haus)
used to form various declined adjective forms, notably the nominative/accusative feminine singular
schön → die schöne Frau
used to form the 1st person singular present indicative (and subjunctive) of a verb
gehen (geh- + -en) → ich gehe (colloquial or poetic: ich geh)
used to form the 3rd person singular present subjunctive of a verb
gehen → er gehe
used to form the 1st and 3rd person singular past subjunctive of a verb
ging → ich ginge, er ginge
-e.et:
From Middle High German -e, a merger of various Old High German vocalic inflectional suffixes.
Further information on -e as noun plural suffix
The plural suffix -e derives from a merger of Old High German -a and -i. Neuters usually remained unchanged in the no…

s: derives demonyms from names of regions and countries
Schweden (“Sweden”) + -e → Schwede (“Swede”)
Mongolei (“Mongolia”) + -e → Mongole (“Mongolian”)
-ist; derives personal nouns from terms for scientific fields of Greek origin
Ornithologie (“ornithology”) + -e → Ornithologe (“ornithologist”)
Logopädie (“speech therapy”) + -e → Logopäde (“speech therapist”)
derives alternative forms of certain personal nouns, particularly of weak loanwords
Katholik + -e → Katholike
Lakai + -e → Lakaie
directly derives loanwords of personal nouns
Dutch matroos + -e → Matrose
-e.et: From Middle High German -e, from Old High German -o, from Proto-West Germanic *-ō, from Proto-Germanic *-ô.
